lesson.title: Where Electron Flow Becomes ATP
lesson.summary: Oxidative phosphorylation is the umbrella process that couples electron transport chain activity to ATP synthase, converting the energy released by electrons flowing to oxygen into newly made ATP.
lesson.body:
Oxidative phosphorylation is the term for the combined process that accounts for the overwhelming majority of ATP produced during cellular respiration, roughly 90 percent of the total. The name describes exactly what happens: phosphorylation, the attachment of a phosphate group to ADP to make ATP, driven by oxidation, the flow of electrons toward oxygen through the electron transport chain. Unlike substrate-level phosphorylation, where an enzyme transfers a phosphate directly from one molecule to another in a single step, oxidative phosphorylation is indirect, requiring an intact membrane and two physically separate but coupled machines working in sequence.

The first machine is the electron transport chain itself, which uses the energy released as electrons move from NADH and FADH2 down to oxygen to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, building up the steep gradient described in the previous section. The second machine is ATP synthase, a remarkable enzyme that spans the inner membrane and functions almost like a turbine. As protons flow back down their concentration gradient through a channel in ATP synthase, that flow physically spins part of the enzyme, and the mechanical rotation drives the chemical bonding of a free phosphate group to ADP, producing ATP. This link between a physical process, proton flow, and a chemical one, ATP synthesis, is what makes oxidative phosphorylation mechanistically different from anything else in this chapter.

It is important to be precise about the word coupling here. The electron transport chain's proton pumping and ATP synthase's ATP production are separate physical events connected only by the proton gradient sitting between them. This is why cyanide is lethal: it blocks Complex IV, stopping electron flow to oxygen, which stops proton pumping, which collapses ATP synthase's fuel supply, even though ATP synthase itself is never directly poisoned. It is also why certain uncoupling agents, both natural, like the protein thermogenin in brown fat, and synthetic, can let protons leak back across the membrane without passing through ATP synthase, releasing the stored energy as heat instead of ATP.

Oxidative phosphorylation depends on every stage covered earlier in this chapter feeding it a steady supply of electrons. Glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle together contribute 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 per glucose molecule, and it is the oxidation of those carriers back to NAD+ and FAD, releasing their electrons into the transport chain, that ultimately powers the vast majority of ATP synthesis. Because ATP synthase requires the mechanical structure and existing electrochemical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane to function, oxidative phosphorylation cannot happen without an intact, sealed membrane, which is one reason mitochondrial damage is so metabolically catastrophic for a cell. The precise mechanism by which the proton gradient itself gets built and spent, chemiosmosis, is worth examining in its own right next.
